practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: A Pond Study
practice.passage: A class studied a small pond near its school. Students recorded water temperature, counted visible organisms from the bank, and drew a model of a food web. Because the first visit happened after rain, they wondered whether that single visit represented typical conditions. They returned at the same time of day during three later weeks. Their records were not identical. One student wanted to erase the unusual measurements, but her partner argued that differences could be useful evidence. The group kept the records and described the limits of its method: it had observed only one pond and had not counted organisms beneath the water. Their report distinguished observations from explanations. "We saw fewer insects" was an observation; "the cooler temperature caused the change" was a hypothesis that needed further testing. The study taught the class that careful questions are as important as confident conclusions.

items.prompt: Identify the dependent clause: "Although it rained, we recorded the temperature."
items.answer: Although it rained

items.prompt: Why is the statement about cooler temperature a hypothesis rather than an observation?
items.answer: The class measured temperature and insect counts but did not establish that temperature caused the change.

items.prompt: How does carbon move from atmosphere into living plants?
items.answer: Photosynthesis incorporates carbon dioxide into organic molecules.

items.prompt: Why is the water cycle a cycle rather than a one-way path?
items.answer: Water moves among reservoirs through repeated processes.

practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: A Pond Study
practice.passage: A class studied a small pond near its school. Students recorded water temperature, counted visible organisms from the bank, and drew a model of a food web. Because the first visit happened after rain, they wondered whether that single visit represented typical conditions. They returned at the same time of day during three later weeks. Their records were not identical. One student wanted to erase the unusual measurements, but her partner argued that differences could be useful evidence. The group kept the records and described the limits of its method: it had observed only one pond and had not counted organisms beneath the water. Their report distinguished observations from explanations. "We saw fewer insects" was an observation; "the cooler temperature caused the change" was a hypothesis that needed further testing. The study taught the class that careful questions are as important as confident conclusions.

items.prompt: What do nitrogen-fixing microorganisms do?

items.prompt: How do photosynthesis and respiration relate to oxygen?

practice.passage: Maya wanted a quiet place to read outside. She asked the librarian if the empty corner of the courtyard could become a garden. First, Maya measured the space. Next, she drew a plan with a path and two benches. Her friends brought seed packets, and an adult helped them plant. A week later, Maya noticed that the plants beside the wall were dry. She moved the watering can closer to them and made a watering chart. By spring, visitors were reading beside green leaves. Maya learned that a good plan needs careful observation as well as enthusiasm.

items.answer: The plants beside the wall were dry, so she needed to organize watering.

practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: A Pond Study
practice.passage: A class studied a small pond near its school. Students recorded water temperature, counted visible organisms from the bank, and drew a model of a food web. Because the first visit happened after rain, they wondered whether that single visit represented typical conditions. They returned at the same time of day during three later weeks. Their records were not identical. One student wanted to erase the unusual measurements, but her partner argued that differences could be useful evidence. The group kept the records and described the limits of its method: it had observed only one pond and had not counted organisms beneath the water. Their report distinguished observations from explanations. "We saw fewer insects" was an observation; "the cooler temperature caused the change" was a hypothesis that needed further testing. The study taught the class that careful questions are as important as confident conclusions.

items.prompt: State a central idea or theme of the passage.
items.answer: Good scientific explanations distinguish evidence, hypotheses, and limitations.

items.prompt: Why is the statement about cooler temperature a hypothesis rather than an observation?
items.answer: The class measured temperature and insect counts but did not establish that temperature caused the change.

items.prompt: What is the role of photosynthesis in an ecosystem?
items.answer: Use light energy to make organic molecules from carbon dioxide and water.

items.prompt: What does cellular respiration do?
items.answer: Release usable energy from organic molecules; aerobic respiration uses oxygen.

practice.passage_title: A Pond Study
practice.passage: A class studied a small pond near its school. Students recorded water temperature, counted visible organisms from the bank, and drew a model of a food web. Because the first visit happened after rain, they wondered whether that single visit represented typical conditions. They returned at the same time of day during three later weeks. Their records were not identical. One student wanted to erase the unusual measurements, but her partner argued that differences could be useful evidence. The group kept the records and described the limits of its method: it had observed only one pond and had not counted organisms beneath the water. Their report distinguished observations from explanations. "We saw fewer insects" was an observation; "the cooler temperature caused the change" was a hypothesis that needed further testing. The study taught the class that careful questions are as important as confident conclusions.

Finally, an adult butterfly emerged. Students recorded dates and made drawings instead of touching the animals. One student wrote that a butterfly is simply a small bird. The teacher asked the class to check its evidence. Their notes showed an insect with six legs, not a bird with two. Careful records helped them correct the mistake. Watching one animal did not tell them everything about every butterfly, but it gave them a useful beginning.

items.prompt: State a central idea or theme of the passage.
items.answer: Observations help students understand a life cycle and correct mistakes.

items.prompt: Why did students record dates and drawings?
items.answer: To preserve observations/evidence of the life cycle.

items.prompt: What are common stages in a flowering plant life cycle?
items.answer: Seed, germination, growth, flowering, and new seed production.

items.prompt: How does a butterfly life cycle differ from simple growth in size?
items.answer: It includes distinct stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult.

practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: Should the School Reduce Plastic?
practice.passage: The student council proposed replacing some single-use lunch packaging with reusable containers. Its argument began with a clear claim: the school should run a four-week trial before making a permanent purchase. The council’s fictional classroom survey found that 72 of 120 respondents supported the trial. A second source, a cafeteria cost table, estimated that washing reusable containers would require additional time. Supporters argued that the trial could measure both waste and labor instead of assuming that one benefit settled the whole question. Critics worried about lost containers and unequal access to supplies. The proposal responded by lending containers during the trial and counting losses. The council did not claim that a survey proved the policy would work. It used the survey to show interest and proposed collecting direct evidence of costs and waste.

items.prompt: Write a defensible claim about the passage.
items.answer: A limited trial can test a proposal while addressing costs and counterarguments.

items.prompt: What does the survey support, and what does it not prove?
items.answer: It shows interest among respondents; it does not prove the policy will work or represent every student.

items.prompt: What makes a sustainability proposal evidence-based?
items.answer: It connects a defined problem, measured outcomes, and realistic tradeoffs.

items.prompt: Why consider unintended consequences?
items.answer: A solution may shift impacts to another part of a system.

practice.passage: This original retelling draws on the traditional myth. Arachne was a talented weaver who took great pride in her work. When people praised her skill, she insisted that no teacher or goddess deserved any credit. Athena, associated with wisdom and crafts, approached in disguise and advised her to speak with humility. Arachne dismissed the advice and demanded a contest. The two wove remarkable pictures, but their conflict involved more than technical skill: Arachne’s attitude challenged the goddess’s authority. In the traditional ending, Athena transformed Arachne into a spider, forever connected with weaving. Readers can admire Arachne’s ability while questioning her boastfulness and the severity of the punishment. The story invites discussion of pride, power, artistic skill, and the consequences of refusing advice. A theme is a reasoned interpretation, not simply the name of a topic.

practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: Arachne: an Original Retelling
practice.passage: This original retelling draws on the traditional myth. Arachne was a talented weaver who took great pride in her work. When people praised her skill, she insisted that no teacher or goddess deserved any credit. Athena, associated with wisdom and crafts, approached in disguise and advised her to speak with humility. Arachne dismissed the advice and demanded a contest. The two wove remarkable pictures, but their conflict involved more than technical skill: Arachne’s attitude challenged the goddess’s authority. In the traditional ending, Athena transformed Arachne into a spider, forever connected with weaving. Readers can admire Arachne’s ability while questioning her boastfulness and the severity of the punishment. The story invites discussion of pride, power, artistic skill, and the consequences of refusing advice. A theme is a reasoned interpretation, not simply the name of a topic.

practice.passage_title: Arachne: an Original Retelling
practice.passage: This original retelling draws on the traditional myth. Arachne was a talented weaver who took great pride in her work. When people praised her skill, she insisted that no teacher or goddess deserved any credit. Athena, associated with wisdom and crafts, approached in disguise and advised her to speak with humility. Arachne dismissed the advice and demanded a contest. The two wove remarkable pictures, but their conflict involved more than technical skill: Arachne’s attitude challenged the goddess’s authority. In the traditional ending, Athena transformed Arachne into a spider, forever connected with weaving. Readers can admire Arachne’s ability while questioning her boastfulness and the severity of the punishment. The story invites discussion of pride, power, artistic skill, and the consequences of refusing advice. A theme is a reasoned interpretation, not simply the name of a topic.

practice.passage: In this original historical fiction, an apprentice watched an experienced builder inspect a Roman-style stone bridge. The apprentice wanted to remove the wooden supports as soon as the final stone was placed. "A finished appearance is not enough," the builder warned. Together they replaced it and repeated the inspection. Later, the apprentice wrote that the delay had been the most important part of the work. The scene does not establish facts about a particular ancient builder; it uses an imagined conversation to explore patience and responsibility. practice.passage_title: The Bridge Apprentice
practice.passage:
In this original historical fiction, an apprentice watched an experienced builder inspect a Roman-style stone bridge. The apprentice wanted to remove the wooden supports as soon as the final stone was placed. "A finished appearance is not enough," the builder warned. He checked the arch and explained how its stones pressed against one another and transferred forces toward the supports. The apprentice grew impatient, but a cracked stone changed her mind. Together they replaced it and repeated the inspection. Later, the apprentice wrote that the delay had been the most important part of the work. The scene does not establish facts about a particular ancient builder; it uses an imagined conversation to explore patience and responsibility. Readers should distinguish the fictional characters from historical claims, such as the Romans’ use of arches in engineering.
Background for comparison: Hermes in Greek tradition and Mercury in Roman tradition are messengers associated with travel.

items.answer: Finding a cracked stone.

items.prompt: How do exothermic and endothermic reactions differ?
items.answer: Exothermic transfers energy to surroundings; endothermic absorbs energy from surroundings.

items.prompt: Why can a reaction’s surroundings change temperature?

The apprentice wanted to remove the wooden supports as soon as the final stone was placed. "A finished appearance is not enough," the builder warned. practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: An Argument for Trees
practice.passage: A community group argues that a school should plant trees near its outdoor learning area. Its claim is narrower than "trees solve every problem": a carefully chosen location may provide shade and support habitat. Its proposal recommends consulting knowledgeable staff, selecting a suitable location, and comparing costs before planting. An effective response to a counterargument does not mock the people who raise it. Instead, it explains how the plan addresses a reasonable concern or why the evidence supports a different choice. The final paragraph asks the school to try a manageable plan and report the results.

items.prompt: Identify one strong idea you could develop from the passage.

items.prompt: How is the claim limited rather than absolute?

items.prompt: Why do extreme-weather explanations need several kinds of evidence?

Original drama:
[An apprentice arranges metal type on a table.]
APPRENTICE: If we print the same page many times, will every reader agree with it?
PRINTER: Copies spread words, not agreement.
APPRENTICE: Then accuracy matters before the first copy.
[The printer points to a misplaced letter.]
PRINTER: And readers must question what they read.

Informational companion: In early modern Europe, printing made it possible to reproduce texts more quickly than copying each one by hand. Printed works helped ideas circulate, including religious, scientific, and artistic arguments. Access remained uneven; not everyone could read or obtain books. Greater circulation did not guarantee that every claim was true. Scholars therefore needed observation, reasoning, and the comparison of sources as well as access to texts.

practice.title: ELA
practice.passage_title: A History Portfolio
practice.passage: A student created a portfolio about how travel and communication changed societies. She began with a research question rather than a list of famous people: How did networks connect communities, and whose experiences were left out of the usual accounts? She compared a map, a trade-route reading, and a translated historical account. Her notes separated quotations, paraphrases, and her own interpretations. When two accounts disagreed, she recorded their authors, purposes, and contexts instead of choosing the more dramatic version. The final presentation used a timeline but did not imply that every change happened everywhere at once. It included an argument supported by evidence and a section explaining limitations. The student concluded that a strong portfolio shows not only a polished product but also how the researcher checked and revised the work.

items.prompt: Write a brief revision/presentation plan with an opening, two supporting points, and a closing.
items.answer: Clear main idea, two accurate relevant supporting points, logical closing.

items.prompt: Why does the timeline need explanation?
items.answer: Changes did not happen at the same time or in the same way everywhere.
